title: John Galliano Announced As Subject Of 2027 Met Gala And Costume Institute Exhibition
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Sets All-Time First-Day High With $167M+ U.S., Could Beat 'Avengers: Endgame' $357M Weekend Record Read the full story By Robert Lang Robert Lang Photo Editor/Arts & Culture Writer More Stories By Robert Denis Villeneuve & Vija Celmins Announced as 2026 LACMA Art+Film Gala Honorees ‘Romy And Michele’ Sequel Begins Production With Original Costume Designer Mona May The Frontier Lives On: Why MoMA Is Revisiting Hollywood’s Greatest Westerns View All July 31, 2026 3:25pm Anna Wintour and John Galliano at the Dior fashion show as part of Haute Couture Spring/Summer 2026 held at the Musée Rodin Swan Gallet/PMC The Metropolitan Museum of Art said Friday that John Galliano will be the subject of its landmark spring 2027 Costume Institute exhibition, John Galliano: Horizons , with the annual Met Gala set to celebrate the acclaimed British designer’s influence on fashion while also confronting the controversy that reshaped his career. Related Stories Culture Met Gala 2026 Photos: Best Of The Red Carpet From Beyoncé, Madonna, Rihanna, Sabrina Carpenter And Teyana Taylor To Janelle Monáe Culture Met Gala 2025 Photos: Best Of The Red Carpet Galliano becomes just the third living designer to receive a solo exhibition at The Met, following Yves Saint Laurent in 1983 and Rei Kawakubo of Comme des Garçons in 2017. Opening in spring 2027, the exhibition marks the first major museum retrospective to examine the full breadth of Galliano’s four-decade career, bringing together garments, accessories, sketches, research books, archival materials and toiles that trace his creative evolution from his celebrated 1984 Central Saint Martins graduation collection through his tenures at Givenchy, Christian Dior and Maison Margiela. Drawing extensively from the Costume Institute’s collection — the largest holding of Galliano’s work in the world — the exhibition culminates with his acclaimed Spring/Summer 2024 Maison Margiela Artisanal collection, hailed by many critics as one of the defining couture presentations of the decade. Watch on Deadline John Galliano poses with models during the Christian Dior Haute Couture fashion show for A/W 2009-10 on July 6, 2009, in Paris. Pascal Le Segretain/Getty Images Beyond celebrating Galliano’s creative achievements, the exhibition also will directly examine the racist, antisemitic and anti-Asian remarks that led to his dismissal from Christian Dior and his namesake label in 2011, as well as his conviction by a Paris court for public insults based on race, religion, ethnicity or origin. Organizers say the exhibition will explore the relationship between artistic achievement and ethical accountability, rather than presenting a traditional narrative of downfall and redemption. “John Galliano has exerted a profound influence on fashion over the past four decades,” said Max Hollein, The Met’s Marina Kellen French Director and CEO. “His work brings historical inquiry, artistic imagination, theatrical expression and technical experimentation into dynamic relation. Drawing upon the depth of The Costume Institute’s scholarship and the breadth of The Met’s collections, John Galliano: Horizons will offer an expansive examination of his creative practice while attending closely to the historical, cultural and ethical circumstances through which his work is understood.” The exhibition is curated by Andrew Bolton, Curator in Charge of the Costume Institute, who has chronicled Galliano’s career through scholarship and previous exhibitions. Stevie Nicks wore a custom look designed by John Galliano for Zara at The 2026 Met Gala Michael Buckner/Penske Media via Getty Images “Every Galliano collection begins as a journey among things separated by time, place or medium: portrait and posture, silhouette and story, memory and material,” Bolton said. “ Horizons approaches fashion as a form of cartography, mapping not territories but affinities, tensions and transformations. It traces how images become ideas, ideas become material and material becomes emotion. Yet a horizon reveals not only what lies before us but also where we stand.” He added that the exhibition will examine “both how Galliano has remapped the world through fashion and how his conduct, its consequences and changing cultural values have reshaped our understanding of his work.” John Galliano and Charlize Theron attend the Metropolitan Museum of Art Costume Institute Benefit Gala: Anglomania at the Metropolitan Museum of Art on May 1, 2006, in New York City Evan Agostini/Getty Images The exhibition will unfold across three thematic sections. The opening movement, “Bearings,” presents a chronological overview of Galliano’s career while directly addressing the events surrounding his 2010 and 2011 conduct, his dismissal from Dior, his treatment for substance addiction and the continuing evolution of his public legacy. The second gallery, “Horizons,” explores the designer’s enduring inspirations — from history and geography to art, performance and storytelling — revealing how disparate cultural references are transformed into richly imaginative collections. The final section, “Atlas of Transformation,” offers an unprecedented look inside Galliano’s creative process through original research books, sketches, fittings, toiles and finished garments, illustrating how concepts evolve into some of fashion’s most celebrated designs. The exhibition has been organized by Bolton with the assistance of Costume Institute staff Stephanie Kramer and Emily Mushaben, with exhibition design by 1009. John Galliano’s Paris Fashion Week Womenswear Spring/Summer 2016 on October 4, 2015 Pascal Le Segretain/Getty Images As is tradition, John Galliano: Horizons will serve as the centerpiece of the 2027 Met Gala, where the fashion industry’s biggest names are expected to interpret the exhibition’s themes on the museum’s iconic steps. The gala’s official dress code, co-chairs and host committee will be announced at a later date. The announcement follows a string of recent Costume Institute exhibitions spotlighting influential designers and fashion movements, but John Galliano: Horizons is poised to become one of the museum’s most closely watched exhibitions for its willingness to examine both extraordinary artistic innovation and the enduring questions surrounding legacy, accountability and cultural memory. The show will be on view at The Met Fifth Avenue from May 9, 2027-January 9, 2028. The Pima County Sheriff’s Department released the notes in hopes of generating new leads in the case. Related Stories News Savannah Guthrie Posts New Video As Authorities Continue Investigation Into Mother’s Disappearance: “We Will Never Give Up On Her” News Savannah Guthrie Speaks On Latest News Of Missing Mother: “We Are In Agony” The first note was sent a day after her disappearance from someone who claimed they have her, and that “she is safe but scared” and would not be released until payment, $4 million in bitcoin, is received, according to the full messages released by the Pima County Sheriff’s Department and the FBI Phoenix Field Office on Friday. The note, addressed to her daughter, Today co-host Savannah Guthrie , said she would be held for a maximum of seven days. The second note, sent Feb. 6 to Tucson news outlet KOLD, states that Guthrie died shortly after she was taken. Watch on Deadline “We did not fully grasp the seriousness of her physical condition,” the note reads. “We never intended to hurt her, that was not our intention. She perished shortly after she was taken. We believe it was heart related. She is buried in nature now. Nothing you could have done could have changed the outcome. We want your family to know this and hope you all can find peace. We are truly sorry.” Investigators believe that someone who knows or has interacted with the writer of the notes — including a friend, family member, co-worker, classmate or acquaintance — may have information that could help identify the person responsible and may have chosen to stay silent because of personal relationships, or safety concerns, and are urging them to come forward. The 84-year-old Guthrie went missing from her home near Tucson early February 1. The FBI has said her disappearance is being investigated as a kidnapping for ransom. Anyone with information is urged to contact 1-800-CALL-FBI (1-800-225-5324). The Guthrie family is also offering a $1 million reward for the return of their mother. title: Tom Corson Promoted at Warner Music After Latest C-Suite Shake Up
full_text: × Skip to main content By Ethan Millman Plus Icon Ethan Millman Music Editor View All July 31, 2026 3:03pm Armin Zerza and Tom Corson Gonzalo Marroquin/Getty Images; Presley Ann/Getty Images Warner Music Group COO and CFO Armin Zerza is stepping down from his role, the company announced on Friday, noting that the executive has decided to leave for “personal reasons.” Warner Records COO Tom Corson will replace Zerza WMG’s as COO, and the company is starting a search for its next CFO. Zerza “will remain available to the company through the end of the fiscal year to ensure a seamless transition,” WMG said. Louis Dickler, WMG’s SVP, Global Controller and Chief Accounting Officer will serve as interim CFO while the company looks for a replacement. It’s a sudden departure for Zerza given that he joined the record company just over a year ago in April of 2025, and he was given the joint role as COO as well just over two months ago. Zerza’s successor will be WMG’s fourth CEO since 2023. Longtime CFO Eric Levin retired in 2023, succeeded by former ESPN and Disney executive Bryan Castellani before Zerza’s appointment in 2025. “Armin has been an instrumental leader and member of the executive team during a crucial period of growth and transformation,” WMG CEO Robert Kyncl said in a statement. “We thank Armin for his outstanding business and financial leadership and enduring contributions to WMG, and we wish him all the best.” Corson , meanwhile, is one of the most respected record executives in the music industry. Before joining Warner, he was the president and COO of RCA Music Group. With Warner Records CEO Aaron Bay-Schuck, the duo led a respected turnaround for the storied label, garnering a reputation in the record business for a strong artist development system with stars like Zach Bryan, Benson Boone and Sombr . With Corson moving to the corporate posting, following the transitional period, Bay-Schuck will helm Warner Records alone. “It’s an honor to step into this role during such a transformative era for both our company and the industry at large,” Corson said in a statement. “A huge thanks to Robert for the opportunity, as well as to Aaron and the Warner Records team for the unforgettable run. I’m looking forward to building on our momentum, turbocharging operations, and creating even more impactful opportunities for our incredible artists and songwriters worldwide.” As Kyncl said of Corson’s appointment: Tom is one of the most dynamic, respected, and effective executives in the music business, and a fierce champion of talent. Together with Aaron, he’s helped architect Warner Records’ resurgence, and we’ll leverage his vision, disciplined execution, and deep experience across the entire company as we continue to deliver for our artists and songwriters while achieving our top and bottom line goals.” THR

title: ‘Cape Fear’ Creator Nick Antosca on That Shocking Final Sequence and Making Big Changes From Scorsese’s Version
full_text: Jul 31, 2026 3:00pm PT ‘Cape Fear’ Creator Nick Antosca on That Shocking Final Sequence and Making Big Changes From Scorsese’s Version By Daniel D'Addario Plus Icon Daniel D'Addario Chief TV Critic DPD_ Latest Evan Rachel Wood Says ‘It’s Sad’ Not to Be Asked Back for ‘Practical Magic 2’ After Offering to Return: ‘It Seems Like They’re Not Following the Book’ 4 days ago ‘Am I Supposed to Be a Comedian?’: Donald Trump’s Bizarre White House Correspondent’s Dinner Speech Had Few Laughing 6 days ago How ‘Cape Fear,’ Apple TV’s Timely Adaptation, Became Summer’s Grisliest Hit 1 week ago See All SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers for “The Executioners,” the finale of “ Cape Fear ,” now streaming on Apple TV . In the final moments of “Cape Fear,” Anna Bowden realizes that she’ll never truly be free of the man who’s been stalking her family. The Bowden family has defeated Max Cady (Javier Bardem), the ex-convict who blames Anna (Amy Adams) and her husband Tom (Patrick Wilson) for his incarceration, in an epic battle during which he invaded their home, placed Anna and Tom on “trial” for colluding against him and threatened their children Natalie and Zack (Lily Collias and Joe Anders). Related Stories Jalen Brunson Talks Taylor Swift’s Wedding, Giving Back and Whether the Knicks Will Visit the Trump White House During that intense confrontation, Anna stunned Max with evidence she obtained at his family’s houseboat that his sister Crystal (Juliette Lewis, who also starred as a different character in the 1991 film version of this story) actually committed the murder for which Max was convicted, having killed Max’s pregnant wife, ripping the unborn fetus from her body. Max’s child actually lived, growing nearly into adulthood while Max spent his life mourning him; in a bitter irony, Max killed him in the chaos that ensued at the Cady family boat at the start of the finale. It’s our definitive proof, too, that Max never did what Tom, as prosecutor, put him away for, and Anna, as defense attorney, didn’t block. For all his crimes against the Bowdens, Max began his legal journey as an innocent man. Popular on Variety Javier Bardem in ‘Cape Fear.’ (Apple TV) By the time he’s defeated, Max seems utterly broken; the last we see of this seemingly invulnerable agent of chaos is his sputtering out water on the Bowdens’ deck, ready to be apprehended by the authorities. But the family’s victory is only conditional. After Anna declares, “Let him die in a cage,” sparing Max’s life, we jump ahead in time to a backyard barbecue, echoing the one that, in happier times, opened the series. Back then, the Bowdens were surrounded by friends, but here, it’s only the four family members, trapped in their fortress. We see Natalie watching a true-crime influencer’s video shot just outside their front door before she joins the rest. As Tom prepares their meal, he glances nervously over his shoulder, toward the pool where he nearly died; Zack sits in eerie silence while his parents force bonhomie, joking about keeping the secret of how good his cheeseburgers are. After Tom refers to Anna as a “psychopath” for ordering her burger without cheese, lettuce, or bun, she declares, “Guilty” — and the verbal reminder of just what they’ve suffered through, and how similar they may be to the guilty psychopath they defeated, overcomes Anna’s defenses. She looks over her shoulder, her face beginning to twist in agony and fear, as the film suddenly shifts to a bright-red filter: End of series, though not of Anna’s psychological journey. Nick Antosca created this version of “Cape Fear” — the third onscreen adaptation of John D. MacDonald’s novel “The Executioners,” following big-screen takes in 1962 and 1991 — and co-wrote the finale. He spoke to Variety via Zoom about that shocking final sequence, the revelation of Max’s innocence and what lies ahead for all the Bowdens, including the daughter who may very well be the product of Anna and Max’s years-ago coupling when they were lawyer and client. I was genuinely struck by the final scene of the series, in which the family is speaking in a sort of coded language that they understand implicitly — and we see just how haunted Anna is. Will the family always be haunted, do you think? The Bowden family will always be haunted by Max Cady and the memory of what happened during this story. The 1991 movie has always struck me in terms of its ending narration, where Juliette’s [Lewis’ character] goes, “And then we never spoke of it again,” basically. You’re just like, Yeah, but I bet you thought about it — still thinking about it today. I wanted our version of that energy. That moment when Tom looks over his shoulder — there’s no sound in the mix motivating that. They’re just going to be looking; they’re going to be hearing things. Lily Collias in ‘Cape Fear.’ (Apple TV) Before Natalie joins the family, she’s fiddling with an envelope from a DNA-testing service that she hasn’t opened yet. One wonders, will she ever open it? One does wonder that. She’s also — very intentionally, it’s barely seen, there’s no close-up of it — wearing an ankle bracelet, too. They’re all going to be dealing with the aftermath of stuff that’s gone on, and they’re probably going to have to sell that house, because I don’t know that they’re going to be allowed to practice law in Georgia in the immediate future. I always imagined that coda — that they would be trying to recreate the first scene, where they’re by their pool and having a barbecue, and things are safe and good. The fact that the series ends with Natalie’s parentage still unresolved feels like a real conversation-starter. Do you have in your mind an answer to the question of who Natalie’s father is? Yes, I do. And you wrote with that in mind. Yes. As a viewer I could go either way! I’m glad. It’s interesting that the finale takes place in the Bowden family home, as opposed to, as in the films, on the boat. In a way, Cady’s intrusion into the home feels even more charged. A lot of people asked as we were getting the last scripts in, or even before, “Is the climax of the show going to be a fight on the storm in the houseboat?” I always felt that we needed to go to the houseboat. But it felt like the conclusion of this version of the Bowden story belonged in the domestic space, so we were to bring the storm to them, and put the trial in their own home. That’s what it felt like it needed to be — and that fight in the pool should feel elemental and primal. We’re in the middle of a hurricane, but it’s their home. Amy Adams in ‘Cape Fear.’ (Apple TV) The violence is really gnarly in the final confrontation. I think of myself as pretty strong-stomached, and I really couldn’t watch the scene where Max convinces a drugged Zack to almost bite his own tongue off. That was one of many shots where we spent a lot of time in the editing room being like, “How many frames of this should we show? How much is too much?” That and the head-smash within the prison in Episode 2. One of the more fun experiences I’ve had in the editing room was being in the edit on that with Martin Scorsese on FaceTime with me, going over it, saying, “Yeah, roll the cut a couple frames, right before the head starts to explode.” Just calibrating, you know, to the exact frame, like how we were going to smash that skinhead’s head. I’m curious about the decision to have the Bowden family spare Max’s life. It’s a departure from the 1991 version. In the 1962 version, he lets him live. We were deciding between those two potential endings. In that moment, the Bowdens are clinging to a last shred of social order and moral order that they believe themselves to be part of. They don’t want to kill a man in front of their children. You could argue that, of all the terrible decisions the Bowdens make throughout this season of television, not killing Max is one of the worst decisions that they could make. From a sheerly pragmatic point of view, they will, of course, always wonder if he’s found his way out of prison and is just around the corner! He’s almost certainly going to prison for a long, long time; he has done a lot of verifiably bad stuff. But if somebody else made the show and I’m watching it, I’m going, “Kill him! Please!” Amy Adams and Patrick Wilson in ‘Cape Fear.’ (Apple TV) The previous versions depicted a Max who maybe should not have been found guilty of their crimes due to mitigating circumstances, but were not literally innocent. This Max, we realize, simply did not do the crime for which he was convicted. It flips the story on its head. So he was wrongly convicted of this murder, but he was a really bad guy in general, and prison narrowed and sharpened that darkness within him. It’s all directed right toward the people he blames. It’s interesting that you talk about the evolution of previous Maxes. In the book, he’s not even the client. He’s just a guy Sam saw committing a crime and testified against him — that’s it. Once you get to the ‘91 version, he was his actual client. That was [screenwriter] Wesley Strick’s innovation, which I think is really brilliant. Each innovation takes the moral complexity to a different level. Early in the episode, Anna provokes Max into choking her in public by declaring that he killed his wife and showing compromising videos of his communications with a past mistress. He’s giving a press conference, and she says just the right things to enrage him. It felt in that moment as if she had an intuitive sense of what buttons to push to get him to drop the facade of control. Can you talk about odd bond and mutual understanding they share? They had a bond, to some degree, in the past, and she’s had to hold herself back for most of the series. Once all is lost for her — at the end of Episode 8, where all of her family is scattered to the winds and locked away, and she’s started drinking again, there is a kind of freedom in that. She goes on her adventure in Episode 9, she gets the information, and then she’s able to use that as ammunition at the beginning of Episode 10. It’s because she has nothing to lose anymore, so she’s able to let loose and press all of his buttons. Before that, she still has the veneer of civility holding her back. Having known my share of attorneys, I also recognized in her a desire to use logic and reason to puzzle her way out of Max stalking her. It seemed to me she triumphed when she started playing according to Max’s own terms. The Bowdens are frustrating for a while, because they want to believe that they’ve got it under control. But I think it’s the case that — like, in your own life, you don’t want to believe things are as bad as they are. Would you move right away? Would you uproot your family and get out? I don’t think you would do that instantly. It’s hard to make big moves in life, sometimes, until it’s too late. Moving is really hard! At the beginning of Episode 3, there’s a scene where random people come into their backyard, and Tom just goes out to talk to them. When we were writing that episode, we were thinking “What are the things that make it feel like your space is permeable? Like you’re under threat?” Around that time, I was at my house, and I walked out into my backyard, and there were some people there. It was just like the show, although I don’t have a castle in Georgia. I was like, “What are you doing here?” and we had this crazy conversation. Later, when the police came, they were like, “Why did you just go up and talk to people who were in your yard hanging out? When that happens, call the police.” But I don’t know. You don’t necessarily think about your own life in the way you would if you were watching characters on TV. You don’t take action that way sometimes until you’re like, Oh, yeah, I guess that really was a threat. I think among the most powerful elements of the series is that the Bowdens are slow to take action in part because they think of themselves as fundamentally good, despite some lapses in the past. Max thrusting his perspective at them forces them to consider how different they really are from Max — that’s very potent. There’s an energy of collective guilt and “No, no, I’m a good person” that feels like part of the culture of modern-day America. That came by osmosis into the show. Do you think the Bowdens are bad people? I think they’re complicated people. They’re very flawed people. This interview has been edited and condensed. Jay Maidment It looks like Tom Holland ’s spoiler of yore — teasing Spider-Man in space for Avengers: Infinity War (2018) alongside the Guardians of the Galaxy (2014) cast — can take on new meaning with the post-credit scene at the end of Spider-Man: Brand New Day . There is just one short snippet after all of the credits have rolled in the movie, so be prepared to settle in all the way until the songs in the film are listed. Related Stories News Sadie Sink’s Role In ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Explained News Amy Pascal On Tom Holland’s Spider-Man & Tom Hardy’s Venom Crossover: “We Have Hope” The bookend of the film shows Ned’s (Jacob Batalon) Spider-Man tracker app interface with a voice alerting the user to a new location for the webslinger. The mask icon that denotes Spidey’s location on a pixelated GPS map, that looks like older videogames, pinpoints the superhero somewhere in space. The playful post-credit bit is followed by Marvel ’s signature text declaring that Spider-Man will return, but not naming which title he will appear in next. Avengers: Doomsday , coming December 18, 2026, could include him if viewers consider the post-credits scene from Thunderbolts* which also teases the arrival of other superheroes in space. Watch on Deadline Ned (Jacob Batalon) works on his Spidey Tracker in Columbia Pictures SPIDER-MAN™: BRAND NEW DAY. Photo by: Jay Maidment That teaser hinted at the meeting of the New Avengers and The Fantastic Four after Yelena Belova’s (Florence Pugh) iPad runs a threat scan of outer space and alerts her of an unidentified craft, an extradimensional ship, entering the orbit of Earth-616. Viewers of Fantastic Four: The First Steps will recall that the film is set on Earth-828, and the spaceship in the Thunderbolts* post-credit scene looks awfully familiar, so it seems that the quartet will join forces with Avengers and New Avengers, or, jokingly, knockoff Avengerz. The projectile rotates to show its blue-backed number four emblazoned on the side. Furthermore, one post-credit scene of Fantastic Four: The First Steps (2025) teases Dr. Victor von Doom (Robert Downey Jr.) meeting Franklin, Sue Storm (Vanessa Kirby) and Reed Richards’ (Pedro Pascal) baby. This interaction was prefaced by “Four Years Later” in the signature Marvel post-credit text. Sue leaves the couch where she is reading to Franklin to get another book for him, and she returns to see the toddler touching an unmasked Doom’s face, but from an angle that only shows his hooded silhouette, holding the silver mask he usually dons. Back to the Thunderbolts* post-credit scene, a dynamic similar to Captain America: Civil War (2016) could be developing because Yelena, Buckey Barnes (Sebastian Stan), John Walker (Wyatt Russell), Ava Starr aka Ghost (Hannah John-Kamen) and Alexei Shostakov (David Harbour) are lamenting how the new Captain America Sam Wilson (Anthony Mackie) is filing for copyright of the name, Avengers vs. their squad, the New Avengers.

title: Bravo VP Talks Amanda’s TV Future After ‘Summer House’ Exit, West’s Departure and ‘In the City’ Season 2: “I’m Optimistic”
full_text: Skip to main content Andy Cohen with the 'In the City' season one cast. Charles Sykes for Bravo Logo text “Summer should be fun — and summer will be fun,” Kyle Cooke said while closing out the In the City reunion earlier this week. And Bravo is indeed having a busy summer after wrapping the first season of In the City , the Summer House spinoff following a group of friends — including Lindsay Hubbard , Kyle Cooke, Amanda Batula , Danielle Olivera and more — as they navigate friendships, relationships and careers in New York City. Filmed immediately after Summer House season 10, the series captured Amanda and Kyle’s marriage before the pair announced their split in January after 10 years together and four years of marriage. Related Stories TV 'In the City' Reunion Concludes With Part Two: How to Watch 'Summer House' Spinoff's Cast Sit-Down Online TV 'In the City' Reunion Recap: Lindsay and Whitney's Heated Exchange, Amanda Reveals She and West Haven't Said "I Love You" During part two of the reunion, Amanda confronted Kyle and alleged she recently learned he had been unfaithful during their marriage, while Kyle claimed Amanda nearly hit him after he woke her up one morning. The pair also revisited Kyle’s comments from the Summer House reunion about their lack of intimacy, ultimately acknowledging their incompatibilities while reiterating they still care deeply for one another as they continue navigating their divorce. Amanda also found herself in the hot seat with Danielle Olivera, apologizing for calling her a “homewrecker” earlier in the season. Andy Cohen also pointed out the contrast between Amanda’s apology to Danielle and her more defensive exchange with Ciara Miller during the Summer House reunion, where Amanda addressed her relationship with Ciara’s ex and fellow Summer House star, West Wilson. In a conversation with The Hollywood Reporter, Josh Brown, Bravo’s vp of current production, who was in the control room during the In the City reunion, breaks down the episode’s biggest moments, shares where things stand with a potential second season of the spinoff — now one of Bravo’s top three most-watched freshman series of the past five years — discusses Carl Radke’s possible future on the series and offers updates on Summer House season 11, including the show’s new house following the departures of Amanda and West. *** Things picked up where they left off last week with Lindsay and Whitney’s heated exchange. Was there anything that we didn’t see, and did they really leave the reunion still on bad terms? For sure, there’s more material, but there were no more twists and turns that viewers didn’t see. Viewers definitely got a true picture of what happened at the reunion. I don’t know if they left on bad terms, but I would call it unresolved terms. I think there will be more to work out in their friendship in real life. Lindsay was quite activated the whole reunion, as we know and love her for. The same with her conversation with Danielle. Was it surprising that maybe things were still left on an unresolved note? I was not surprised. I actually thought it was hopeful by the end, at least in my opinion. I work on Summer House as well, and I’ve worked on that series since the beginning. We’ve seen so many twists and turns in the Lindsay and Danielle friendship. So many ups and downs about so many different subjects. From when one of them was in a relationship and one of them was not, to when they were each in relationships, and now both moms, which is fascinating. So, I will never count either of them out to try and work out their friendship. They’ve had a long history together, and personally, I think it’d be great to see them continue to get to a good place. Lindsay had called out Danielle for not being as open in front of the cameras about her relationship. Could that impact her returning to the series? That wouldn’t affect how we move forward with Danielle in a future season. It’s more something for Lindsay and Danielle to work out, and if others in the cast take issue with anything, it’s more for them to work out as a friend group. What is your take on the color of Danielle’s dress to Yvonne’s wedding reception? Was it pink? Was it white? Did production warn her to maybe choose something else to wear? Well, by coincidence, I happened to be at that scene, and I will say that colors are not my specialty. ( Laughs. ) It looked — it was borderline. Let’s put it that way. In some light, it looked pink, and in some light, it looked a little bit closer to white. So, I could see both sides. What did you think about Whitney and Kenny’s performance at the reunion and how they held their own — especially in their arguments with Lindsay? I think that everyone gave great effort at the In the City reunion overall. I was proud of the cast. This was a first season. We don’t always have reunions in first seasons of Bravo series, and we had a very veteran cast in Kyle, Amanda and Lindsay. Even Danielle is extremely veteran. Then we had someone like Andrea, who’s kind of in the middle of experience. We had some very, very new cast members, and I feel like the cast did great in terms of how they did at the reunion. So we’re happy with it. There was discourse surrounding Amanda’s performance at the Summer House reunion , and she addressed it at the In the City reunion. What was her energy like that day? Did you notice a shift where she approached this differently? I did notice a huge difference from the minute each reunion started. I think Amanda was very scared at the Summer House reunion. I think she was not sure what it was going to be like and knew she was going to be asked a lot of tough questions by some of her fellow castmates about certain things that happened in that friend group. Here on In the City, there were a lot of questions for Amanda, but they were ultimately about the In the City friend group, her marriage and the fallout so the subjects and the stakes of the conversations were really different and I think she felt that going into each reunion, so I do think you saw a very different Amanda in each reunion. She seemed more relaxed here for sure. Amanda had a big reveal when it came to Kyle; she said she found out recently that he was unfaithful in their marriage. He seemed to be shocked by that. Was there anything that viewers didn’t see with that conversation? I think that was surprising to everyone, both, you know, her and Kyle’s fellow castmates and to producers behind the scenes. There wasn’t more information given at the reunion that viewers didn’t see. Andy said that Amanda’s apology to Danielle was very sincere and remorseful, and that it would have gone a long way with Ciara. Was it surprising to see her apologize to Danielle like that? Do you think that will change how some viewers perceived her from the Summer House reunion? I don’t know if it will change how they perceive her. I really don’t. I think viewers would appreciate that she apologized to Danielle. I was not surprised that she apologized to Danielle. I think what I was maybe more surprised about was the lack of a true-feeling apology to Ciara. I think that was surprising to everyone behind the scenes back at the Summer House reunion. Kyle Cooke, Ciara Miller, Andy Cohen, Amanda Batula and West Wilson at the Summer House season 10 reunion. Jocelyn Prescod/Bravo Moving forward, if In the City gets a second season, how do you think it will play out with Kyle and Amanda’s dynamic? Can they both be on the show? That is a very good question. I think, like Summer House, we approach things organically, and so we have to go by the facts on the ground, so to speak. I really don’t know what would happen if we are to get a season two. The one thing I would say is that, as viewers have seen on Summer House and In the City, both Kyle and Amanda are making a sincere effort to be friends post-marriage, even though they’re still technically married. They both really care about each other. I think viewers felt that at the reunion. What’s the status of season two right now? Have you heard anything? It’s too early to say. We just finished airing the season, and we’re really happy with the performance of the series in its first season. Bravo just released a big announcement about ratings in the past week or so, and In the City was included in that touting its performance for season one. So I’m optimistic. A few days after In the City’s reunion filmed, it was announced that West was leaving Summer House . Two weeks after that, it was announced that Amanda was leaving Summer House . What is Amanda’s future on TV? Could she still be part of a future season of In the City? Could we see West join? If I’m being honest, I think it’s too early to talk about that. We just finished airing the season, but we always approach things organically and by the facts on the ground. So, anything’s always possible, but there’s no plans for anything at this time about anything I should say, just because we’re still reacting to finishing airing the season. We’re getting our heads around where we go from here, so it’s too early to talk about casting for season two. Have you had any talks with Amanda about whether she’d even want to return to TV in the future? I have not — we have not. It’s just too soon to be talking about that. We are so appreciative of everything she’s done so far, and we really care about her. But it’s just too early to be having any talks like that. It’s premature. When do you think that process for In the City will start? I would say by the end of the summer for sure. We’ll definitely know a lot more within a month. Fans have been begging for Carl to be on In the City as a cast member. Is that something that you’d be open to? We obviously love Carl, and he made an appearance on In the City. In the City, I think, is a very different subject than Summer House. It’s about people who are sort of on the edge of leaping into a big adult decision, and they’re not quite sure which way to go on it, which is very different than Summer House. And so, I would say for anyone, that would have to be part of the equation that we factor in on the show in terms of their bigger participation on the show for Carl or anyone else. But Carl, of course, is a very organic part of the group, even In the City cast. So, if there’s a reason and if it feels organic, we always love Carl. After everything that’s happened with Summer House , is there anything that you learned from these experiences that you’ll apply to either the next season of Summer House or a potential second season of In the City? This was the ultimate sign of how willing this cast is to really talk about what’s really going on in their real lives. Obviously, last season was a very tough season in a lot of ways. Or really, it was the fallout from the season. It wasn’t necessarily things that happened on Summer House that were as tough, but it was what happened after the season and the reunion. The fact that we are back on Summer House the very next summer for another season, obviously, we’ve had some changes on the show in terms of who’s there, but the fact that we’re back with our forecast and moving forward and having a really fun, exciting summer says a lot about this group and the real friendships that are approaching over a decade for some of them. We hope to build that in a very separate way on In the City, should we get a green light. We want this real friend group that hangs out 12 months a year and not just showing up for filming. So, if that cast is willing to go there, we’re hopeful. West has said that his exit was mutual. Is that correct, or is there anything you can share about that? Yeah, I mean, especially with something like Summer House, it has to be the right fit. It has to feel real because they’re housemates. This is not like a house reality show where we bring in 10 strangers and see what happens when these 10 strangers get to know each other. This is a real friend group and an organic friend group, and so if someone doesn’t fit organically in the group, there’s sort of nothing that can be done. I’m sure West quickly recognized that. I’ve not spoken to him about this, but I would guess that he would not be interested in pushing his way into any friend group. He wants to live his life as well. Was it similar with Amanda, where it felt like there was just too much damage done and things couldn’t return to how they were with the group? Yeah, that’s exactly what I would say. Most episodes, every morning, they have to wake up and have breakfast together. You can’t have breakfast with someone that you don’t want to be there — it doesn’t make any sense for a show about a Hamptons house share. Obviously people will go through their ups and downs and their conflicts, and maybe once in a while, I’m sure a cast member is thinking, “Wow, I really wish I weren’t facing this person over my omelet right now.” But in the end, they have to have breakfast together. So, it’s going to feel forced if it’s not an organic friend group of people who, at their core, like each other as friends. Is it true there’s a new house for Summer House season 11? We can say that we’re not in the same house as last season. That’s true. So I think that’s great. It’s a new chapter. It was a wonderful house that we had for years, but I don’t know how the cast would have felt being back in that same house. We decided to get a different house way before this scandal and news broke, but I’m very grateful that we did make that decision because I think it would have been tough for them, some of them, emotionally, to be back in the same house. Can you tease anything about how Ciara is doing this summer? Here’s what I would say: I’m the biggest Ciara fan. So I’m a cheerleader for her in life, including Summer House, but also everything else she’s doing. I feel like Ciara is living her best life, and I think people are going to see a lighter, really fun Ciara who’s not weighed down as much by the conflicts of Summer House past. It’s going to be a really fun summer for her and for us. *** All episodes of In the City season one and 10 seasons of Summer House are streaming on Peacock. title: Olivia Wilde and Cooper Hoffman Used Pain Scale Ratings to Prep BDSM Scenes in ‘I Want Your Sex’: She ‘Hit Him Really Hard and’ It Was ‘Only a Seven or Eight’
full_text: Jul 31, 2026 2:34pm PT Olivia Wilde and Cooper Hoffman Used Pain Scale Ratings to Prep BDSM Scenes in ‘I Want Your Sex’: She ‘Hit Him Really Hard and’ It Was ‘Only a Seven or Eight’ By Anna Tingley Plus Icon Anna Tingley Latest Olivia Wilde and Cooper Hoffman Used Pain Scale Ratings to Prep BDSM Scenes in ‘I Want Your Sex’: She ‘Hit Him Really Hard and’ It Was ‘Only a Seven or Eight’ 13 hours ago You Can Now Land New York’s Toughest Restaurant Reservations Through DoorDash 14 hours ago How to Stream Shark Week Live Online Without Cable 5 days ago See All Cooper Hoffman had never filmed a sex scene before signing on to Gregg Araki’s erotic thriller “ I Want Your Sex .” So when he arrived on set for the first time and found himself surrounded by ball gags, stilettos, whips, chains, dildos and strap-ons, a few first-day jitters were understandable. “Even if you’re nervous to do it, you’re gonna do it,” Hoffman told Variety at the film’s Los Angeles premiere on Tuesday night. “Because there’s no reason to not do anything in this life just because you’re scared.” Related Stories Jalen Brunson Talks Taylor Swift’s Wedding, Giving Back and Whether the Knicks Will Visit the Trump White House Still, how does an actor prepare to strip naked, slip into a maid’s outfit and get spanked with a leather whip? This is just one of many, many kinky situations Hoffman encounters as Elliot, a meek, wide-eyed college graduate who enters into a sadomasochistic relationship with gallery owner Erika Tracey (Olivia Wilde). Popular on Variety Increasingly, the answer comes in the form of an intimacy coordinator — a role that Araki, long known for embracing provocative themes, employed for the first time on this project. The profession, which officially unionized with SAG-AFTRA in 2024, has become an increasingly standard presence on film and television sets. Intimacy coordinator Yehuda Duenyas likens the job to that of a choreographer or stunt coordinator. “If someone is going to get their head blown off, people are like, ‘Go grab the goo gun, get the exploding head with the squibs in it, press the button and boom.’ No one really bats an eye about violence,” he says. “But when it comes to intimacy, everyone gets kind of squishy and weird.” “There are so many things to look after with intimacy scenes that no one really sees,” he continues. “It’s the same way that, with a stunt, you’re not seeing the padding or the fake hits. It just looks real, but you know there’s a lot of movie magic happening behind the scenes.” That movie magic is put to work throughout the film, which uses high-intensity montages to establish the pair’s dom-sub dynamic: Elliot crawling across the floor in pink silk lingerie, taking a spanking in a maid’s outfit, standing fully nude as a hot-pink dildo is lubed up overhead and, during a threesome-gone-wrong, getting handcuffed to a St. Andrew’s cross with a towel stuffed in his mouth. “He might have been terrified, but it wasn’t, ‘I’m terrified, I don’t want to do this.’ It was, ‘I’m terrified, and I do want to do this,'” Duenyas says of Hoffman. “He was more like, ‘Yeah, yeah, it’s the scariest thing I’ve ever done. Let’s do it.'” Below, Duenyas talks about how he prepared Wilde and Hoffman for their most intense on-screen moments, the most challenging scenes to shoot and the film’s overall messaging on sex and experimentation: There are multiple high-intensity montages that establish the nature of Olivia and Cooper’s dom-sub sexual relationship. What would surprise people about what goes into shooting scenes like that? With those montages specifically, we had moments where we would say, “Okay, I’m hitting you this hard. What is that on a scale of one to 10?” Cooper would say, “That’s a zero.” She’d say, “Really?” Then she would go harder, and he’d say, “Okay, that’s a two. That’s a three. That’s a five.” Olivia realized, “I can hit you really hard, and it’s only registering as a seven or an eight.” We had a bunch of little things like that so they could, number one, have a language for communicating about the physicality and, number two, feel like they could talk about what was happening while also making it look good. ©Magnolia Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection Gregg told Variety that Olivia came onto the set with much more experience doing nude scenes, while Cooper was “terrified.” What was your process for making him more comfortable from the beginning? If you’ve ever gone skydiving, you might be terrified, but you really want to go skydiving. You’re there to do it. Or, if you’ve ever jumped off a cliff into water or stood on a high diving board, you’re on top of that thing to do it, even though you’re scared. So, yeah, he might have been terrified, but it wasn’t, “I’m terrified, I don’t want to do this.” It was, “I’m terrified, and I do want to do this.” Is someone terrified because they’re thinking, “This is a no for me. This is a hard boundary, but I’m involved in this thing and I already said yes, so what am I going to do?” Are they biting their nails or is it, “I’m fucking terrified. Let’s do this really well. How are we going to do this?” That was Cooper’s stance. I wouldn’t say he was terrified. If you’ve ever talked to him, he’s super cool and very together. He was more like, “Yeah, yeah, it’s the scariest thing I’ve ever done. Let’s do it.” It was very matter-of-fact. He approaches almost everything he does by diving headfirst into it in this really beautiful way. He’s an incredible performer. How did the dom-sub type of sex scenes differ from the more traditional sex scenes you’re used to working on? Sure, there are differences, but in terms of the way we approach intimacy coordination as a craft, it’s not that different. Olivia had also done a lot of research. Everyone brought what they knew and the type of story they wanted to tell. Gregg obviously did as well. In this particular film, we’re dealing with these very specific, blurry and complicated power dynamics. That’s the story. The story shows up in their relationship, their work lives and their sexual lives together. What was so fun was finding the character of their intimacy together. Every intimate scene we work on has a different type of character, and that was the character for this one. Is it different? Yes. BDSM and these kinds of lifestyle scenes, if you want to call them that, are different from something like a “Heated Rivalry” scene. It’s a different type of intimacy, but we approach it the way we would approach anything else. ©Magnolia Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection I’m guessing one of the main differences is how many props are involved. What was the most challenging scene to work on? The threesome scene, from a blocking and camera-angle perspective, took a minute to figure out. When I say “a minute,” we had a really compressed shooting schedule. We shot all the intimacy within the first five days. We did all of that stuff upfront. Also from an intensity perspective, that scene required a lot. There was a lot to work out. It wasn’t, “Oh my God, this is so hard.” It was a puzzle to put together in terms of the traffic patterns, the handcuffing and how to get out of the handcuffs quickly. Are we fiddling with keys, or are we just getting out of them? There are a lot of little details. Which details are you going to skip for the sake of the story, and which details are you going to keep in to maintain the flavor and the vibe of the story? All of the restraint scenes needed a little more care. Getting an actor into restraints on the St. Andrew’s cross wasn’t that complicated of a scene. But when you have to shoot it from three angles in three different ways, and an actor is strapped to a St. Andrew’s cross, can they get out easily if they need to pee? Gregg recently talked to Variety about Gen Z’s attitude towards sex and what he hoped to accomplish with this film. What are your thoughts on this mission statement? Gregg wants people to go out and argue. He really wants people to argue about it and say, “Well, I thought it was this,” or, “I thought it was that,” or, “I think that’s bullshit,” or, “I think that’s true.” He wants those conversations. I love Gregg, and I’ve loved his work over the years. He has contributed so much. I learned about intimacy through watching Gregg Araki films as a young person. I feel like we owe him for his contribution to intimacy in cinema. He has contributed so much to the film canon. Where would we be without those pieces he has made and the work he has put in? I can’t speak for Gen Z, and I don’t know whether Gen Z is having less or more sex. But I hope people see this film and want to take a chance on love, take a chance on experimentation, take a chance on feeling something and allow themselves to be taken to a place they haven’t been before. title: John Oliver Extends His HBO Contract to Continue ‘Last Week Tonight’ Through 2027
full_text: Jul 31, 2026 2:18pm PT John Oliver Extends His HBO Contract to Continue ‘Last Week Tonight’ Through 2027 By Michael Schneider Plus Icon Michael Schneider Variety Editor at Large franklinavenue Latest John Oliver Extends His HBO Contract to Continue ‘Last Week Tonight’ Through 2027 13 hours ago ‘Stuart Fails to Save the Universe’ Producers on Episode 2’s Surprise Kaley Cuoco Cameo as an Alternate Penny 1 day ago Banijay Americas CEO Ben Samek to Oversee Merged Banijay/All3Media Operations in the U.S. 1 day ago See All HBO Max John Oliver is staying put for now at HBO, no matter whom his “business daddy” might end up being next year. The “ Last Week Tonight With John Oliver” host has extended his contract with the network through the end of 2027, Variety has confirmed. But perhaps because of the ownership uncertainty, Oliver’s extension is only for one year, vs. its usual three-year pickups. Oliver has been vocal on “Last Week Tonight” about his concerns over Paramount Skydance’s proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery: “Yeah, not great news,” he said in a March episode . “In fact, if I may quote anyone who’s ever accidentally sat on their Roku remote, I’m in Paramount now … how the f-ck do I get out of here?’” Related Stories Jalen Brunson Talks Taylor Swift’s Wedding, Giving Back and Whether the Knicks Will Visit the Trump White House When news of Paramount’s desire to take over Warner Bros. first emerged last September, he also had this to say: “Please stay the f-ck away from us. You are not my real business daddy, and you never will be!” At the time, Oliver was critical of Paramount’s settlement with the Trump administration over its baseless lawsuit against CBS’ “60 Minutes.” He has also been critical of Bari Weiss’ takeover of CBS News. Popular on Variety Oliver resumed new episodes of “Last Week Tonight” this week after a summer hiatus , and spent much of the show dissecting Donald Trump’s latest doings — potentially also putting him in the crosshairs of the Trump-friendly Paramount Skydance owners. “Last Week Tonight” was last renewed for three years in December 2023, bringing the show up to this year and its Season 13. “Over the past decade, John and his exceptional team have combined deep research and intelligence with cutting humor to tackle a broad range of subjects, both widely discussed and unconventional,” Casey Bloys, chairman and CEO, HBO & Max Content, said in a statement at the time. “Last Week Tonight” first launched in 2014 and is now in its 13th season. The show has scored 28 Emmys; last year it won the scripted variety series and variety writing categories (where it has dominated for the last eight years). The show also has two Peabody Awards, five Critics Choice Awards, two GLAAD Media Awards, six Writers Guild Awards and eight consecutive PGA Awards. “ Last Week Tonight With John Oliver ” is produced for HBO by Avalon and Peyance Productions; executive producers are Oliver, Tim Carvell, Liz Stanton, Jon Thoday and James Taylor. Director is Paul Pennolino. THR first reported the news of Oliver’s deal extension. Loading comments... title: Wendell Pierce & Erika Woods Break Down Shocking ‘Power Book III: Raising Kanan’ Series Penultimate Episode
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Sets All-Time First-Day High With $167M+ U.S., Could Beat 'Avengers: Endgame' $357M Weekend Record Read the full story By Rosy Cordero Rosy Cordero Associate Editor, TV @SocialRosy More Stories By Rosy Wendell Pierce & Erika Woods Break Down Shocking ‘Power Book III: Raising Kanan’ Series Penultimate Episode Dermot Mulroney To Leave ‘Chicago Fire’ Early In Season 15 Rebecca Hall Officially Joins Netflix Series Based On Dan Brown Novel ‘The Secret Of Secrets’ View All July 31, 2026 2:07pm Wendell Pierce & Erika Woods in Power Book III: Raising Kanan' Season 5 Episode 7 Starz SPOILER ALERT: The following reveals major plot points for Starz ’s Power Book III: Raising Kanan Season 5 Episode 7. With only one episode to go for the series finale of the hit Starz crime drama Power Book II: Raising Kanan , there’s no doubt that there are plenty of bodies yet to be piled up. In last night’s episode—the penultimate of the series—fans witnessed the end of three lives that were mostly unexpected. As I reported this morning, following the early season death of Lou (Malcolm Mays), Raising Kanan killed off his brother Marvin (London Brown) in Episode 7. This ending was not fully a surprise, as the character had accepted his fate and had plans put in motion to protect his daughter Jukebox (Hailey Kilgore). Read Brown’s true post-mortem to learn more about what was going on in Marvin’s head and what could’ve been should he have survived . Related Stories News 'Power Book III: Raising Kanan' Says Goodbye To Major Series Character In Season 5: "I Wish We Could've Gotten One More Season" Casting Claire Foy & Matthew Macfadyen To Lead David Nicholls Novel Adaptation 'You Are Here' For BBC & Starz What I didn’t note in that story is that there were two more significant deaths. Last night, we also said goodbye to Snaps ( Wendell Pierce ) and Pop (Erika Woods), two agents of chaos who joined the fold in Season 3. They were murdered by Juke in a surprise twist following the revelation that they were behind Famous’ (Antonio Ortiz) death in Season 4. Watch on Deadline Pierce and Woods spoke to Deadline about Snaps and Pop’s demise, what it’s like playing a couple as a real-life couple, and why it was perfect that they were shot to death by Juke. DEADLINE: What was the initial attraction for you both to play Snaps and Pop? ERIKA WOODS: Getting to work with Wendell Pierce definitely made it very attractive. I mean, duh. [ Laughs ] For me, that was that was first and foremost. And then getting to play someone on the other side of law, since I’ve always played law enforcement. Getting to play someone so devious and delicious and methodical-it was really challenging and, most of all, fun. WENDELL PIERCE: I just wanted to be a part of the world. They are very specific in the way they develop characters and populate the world of the Power universe. That’s a very rare thing. So, any sort of good writing is always attractive. DEADLINE: When I announced your castings, I learned you are a real-life couple. What was it like working together? WOODS: It was really fun and a great learning experience. And just like with any coworker, it was a great collaboration with not just Wendell, but our nephew Breeze [Shameik Moore] and all the other great characters in the universe. It was the icing on the cake. PIERCE: You do the work as normal. You try to be a great collaborator and be there for your scene partner. And since we know each other really well, it really helps develop the characters a little deeper. DEADLINE: One of my favorite elements of this couple was how they dressed and carried themselves. The costumes were all top-notch. Did you enjoy that as well? WOODS: Yes, it was the other character in the universe; our wardrobe, led by Tsigie White, was another collaborator for us. I absolutely loved it. It helped shape our characters. PIERCE: It lets you know who you are. The clothes are just another variable that lets you know who the character is as a part of the character development. And Tsigie is a great designer. Everything was custom. I really think the work that she did is worthy of awards because people always take it for granted that costuming is not easy, especially when it’s a contemporary show. It really is very specific, very inventive, very creative work with different fabrics. We became known for dressing alike and complementing each other so much so that our characters have become one of the leading characters for Halloween. DEADLINE: Did either of you take anything home as a memento? PIERCE: I did. I had such great hats. I took several hats. You know, the red ostrich and brown leather and all of that. So I have a collection of a few of the hats. WOODS: I definitely did take a pair of boots. Really nice vintage boots that I loved. DEADLINE: Focusing on Episode 7, we all say goodbye to Snaps and Pop after Jukebox murders them. Why was she the right person to kill them? WOODS: I think with Juke it was the element of surprise, which I think was perfect, because Kanan [Mekai Curtis] might have been the obvious choice. I think to have Juke and her discretion and being so methodical, we had no idea we were being followed. She outgained us in the end. I thought that was just genius writing, and very well played. PIERCE: Ultimately, when you are in the game, you always have to have your head on a swivel and watch your back. But it’s almost impossible for anyone to be absolutely perfect. With as long as we have been in the game, and as the OGs, we let our guard down. It takes that one moment of indiscretion and relaxation that puts you in jeopardy. That’s the lesson that’s learned. You pay the consequences for the lifestyle that you lead, and as the saying goes, no one gets out of this life alive. DEADLINE: With the loss of Marvin, Snaps, and Pop, how do you think it will affect the game? PIERCE: The thing I love about the Power Universe is we play with time. This was a prequel set before the original Power, and next we’re seeing Origins , how others come on. We spoke for two seasons about Breeze before we even saw him. So there are opportunities to go back and discover how these people got involved in the game, and what made them an OG. There are flashbacks [on the show]. We saw Lou after he was dead, and we saw scenes leading up to his death. There’s still a lot of history about Snaps and Pop that we don’t know. Snap, Crackle, and Pop. Who’s Crackle? DEADLINE: Wait a minute, there’s a Crackle? WOODS: Yep! PIERCE: You’ll have to wait and see. DEADLINE: It has to be DefCon. PIERCE: We’ll have to wait and see. And what was our relationship with DefCon? Who is DefCon? WOODS: Huh? It would be nice to reveal that in Origins , don’t you think, Rosy? I think that would be a very nice reveal because I can neither confirm nor deny. PIERCE: Ultimately, you have to pay the consequences for your actions. So that’s the lesson in what happens to these characters in this episode. What you do in the dark will ultimately come to light, so you best be careful. There, but by the grace of God, go I. What happened to me can also happen to you. DEADLINE: So what you are teasing is that you both could come back as flashbacks in Power: Origins ? PIERCE: Anything is possible. title: Sheriff in Nancy Guthrie Case Releases Ransom Notes: “She Perished Shortly After She Was Taken”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All July 31, 2026 1:58pm Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos spoke to the media on Feb. 3 in Tucson, Arizona. Jan Sonnenmair/Getty Images Chris Nanos, the sheriff in the Nancy Guthrie kidnapping case, has released a pair of ransom notes initially sent to the CBS affiliate in her home city of Tucson, Arizona. The second of the two notes states that Nancy has “perished.” The notes “purport to have been written by kidnappers,” the Pima County Sheriff’s Department wrote in a press release timed to the six-month anniversary of Nancy’s disappearance . The first note was sent to KOLD-TV 13 News on Feb. 2; Nancy was last seen alive on Jan. 31. Addressed directly to Savannah Guthrie , the first ransom note demands $4 million-$6 million (depending on date of deposit) in Bitcoin for her safe release. It says Nancy is “safe but scared.” Related Stories TV The Reporter Who Won't Give Up On the Nancy Guthrie Kidnapping Story News Nancy Guthrie Ransom Notes Were All Reportedly Fake “Her life is in your hands,” the first note states. The note’s final line offers two details as proof of its legitimacy: “She had a white smart watch on the floor of the foot of her bed and the white flood light in the backyard was destroyed.” Nancy Guthrie is the mother of Today show co-anchor Savannah Guthrie. She was 84 years old at the time of her disappearance. On Feb. 6, a second email sent to the same news outlet’s Tips line states that Nancy has died and “is buried in nature.” The initial deadline for the ransom deposit ($4 million) was Feb. 5; the second deadline ($6 million) was Feb. 9. The second note reads, in full: “Guthrie Family, We did not fully grasp the seriousness of her physical condition. We never intended to hurt her, that was not our intention. She perished shortly after she was taken. We believe it was heart related. She is buried in nature now. Nothing you could have done could have changed the outcome. We want your family to know this and hope you can all find peace. We are truly sorry.” Nancy had a serious heart condition and was without her medication. The ransom notes are posted below. The first Nancy Guthrie ransom note. Pima County Sheriff’s Office The second Nancy Guthrie ransom note. Pima County Sheriff’s Office The Pima County Sheriff’s Department says it is sharing the ransom notes now for the first time publicly in hopes that someone in the public recognizes “distinctive patterns of word choice, syntax and phraseology that reflect the writer’s unique linguistic style.” “They also provide valuable insight into the person’s mindset, motives and the evolution of their tone over time,” the press release continues. “As with the unidentified male depicted in the video, we believe these distinctive linguistic characteristics may be recognizable to someone who knows or has interacted with the notes’ writer. A friend, family member, coworker, classmate or acquaintance may recognize these patterns of expression and possess information that could help identify the individual responsible.” Doorbell videos of the suspected kidnapper were released to the public on Feb. 10. title: Sam Fender and Olivia Dean Have the Longest-Running No. 1 in U.K. History
full_text: × Skip to main content By Ethan Millman Plus Icon Ethan Millman Music Editor View All July 31, 2026 1:36pm Sam Fender and Olivia Dean Samir Hussein/WireImage Sam Fender and Olivia Dean have made history, as the duo has set the new U.K. record for longest run atop the U.K.’s singles chart with their song “Rein Me In,” which has now spent 19 weeks at No. 1, the U.K.’s Official Charts Company announced on Friday. Fender and Dean took the throne from the late Frankie Laine, who’d held the record for over 70 years as his 1953 hit “I Believe” spent 18 weeks atop the chart. “Completely lost for words, thank you so much to Olivia Dean and the fans for making this song the juggernaut that it is,” Fender told the Official Charts company on Friday. “Can’t believe we broke the U.K. record!” Related Stories TV FIFA Boss Infantino Under Fire Over World Cup Sell Off Plans Movies Filmsaaz and Neozoon: Meet Filmmakers With Pseudonyms - and Political Movies - at Locarno “Rein Me In” first made its way onto the U.K. single chart in June of 2025, steadily making its way up the ladder before finally reaching the top this past February. From then, it enjoyed the top spot for 19 non-consecutive weeks, only getting interrupted by Harry Styles’ “American Girls,” Olivia Rodrigo’s “Drop Dead,” Ariana Grande’s “Hate that I Made You Love Me” and Taylor Swift’s “I Knew It, I Knew You.” “Rein Me In” managed to outlast Shakira and Burna Boy’s global smash “Dai Dai,” which is the anthem to the 2026 FIFA World Cup. Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas,” arguably the biggest song of the year in the U.S., reached a new peak at No. 3. Stateside, “Rein Me In” currently sits at 69 on Billboard’s Hot 100 chart. Dean has two top 10 songs in the U.S. herself with “So Easy (To Fall in Love)” and “Man I Need.” THR
